synopsis: Following a foam strike during launch in January 2003, engineers assessed Columbia’s tile damage using the empirical Crater model; the in-flight assessment reported no safety-of-flight issue, and Columbia was lost on re-entry on 1 February 2003 [f7950, f7957, f7958]. The assessed debris was about 400 times the size represented in Crater’s test database, although an early briefing cited 640 times; the model’s conservative bias for small impacts was assumed to persist at this much larger scale [f7582, f14936]. Across the introduction, Chapter 10 and glossary, Columbia is presented as a canonical false-confidence case involving extrapolation beyond a validated domain and human reinterpretation of the result [f192, f7581, f14939]. The interpretation is contested: the investigation board emphasized model validity, while Hale argued that Crater gave a correct warning that management overrode; the booklet records both views [f8192, f15853]. For the heavy off-road program, the lessons are to specify validity envelopes and margins, avoid relying on simulations of physically untested machines, sensors and weather, and communicate caveats plainly; the case also directly drove NASA-STD-7009 [f15854, f15856, f15855, f7962].
